Speaking thus, thousands of warriors intent on slaying one another
fought there like rutting great elephants. (27)
Addressing one another thus, they dispatched [each other] to Yama's abode.
Siddhas and Cāraṇas, all stationed in the sky, (28)
acclaimed them, made merry, and roared like clouds:
“This Dānava slain in battle has been appointed my husband! (29)
This god is your husband; do not set your mind on another’s!
Why are you filled with greed, examining the best of the best? (30)
There is no self-selection here; read the written decree, do not hurry!
Why is your mind discontented? Be satisfied, O beautiful one! (31)
This share is allotted to you by the gods; take him and go home!”
Thus the apsarases there spoke and laughed, (32)
and they quarrelled when a warrior was slain in battle.
Listening repeatedly to that sweet chatter of theirs,
mingled with the clinking of their girdles and bangles, those warriors fought without fear,
and they made all directions resound with prancing and loud slaps. (33–34)
Resounding with musical instruments, elephant trumpeting, prancing, and furious lion-roars,
that battle shone forth, causing terror between gods and Dānavas and bringing an end to life. (35)
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, on the battle, in the Skandapurāṇa.

Sanatkumāra said:
That foremost battle-sacrifice then took place for the sake of sovereignty.
There, the illustrious thousand-eyed god himself was the sacrificer. (1)
Along with the gods, the lord of the gods [was the sacrificer]; his arrows were considered the kuśa grass. / The diverse weapons were the sruva-ladles with which the oblation was offered.

7.9.m: Sanatkumāra said: / The Dānavas’ son Vipracitti, of great illusions, showered Vāyu / with many swift arrows, just like a cloud bearing water with rain. / Covering [him] then, O Vyāsa, bending his bow into a circle, / he shot sharp-pointed arrows, as the ocean [sends forth] locusts. / As streams from a cloud, as moonlight from the moon, / as rays from the sun, as snow from the snow-mountain, / so those swarms of arrows shot forth from the circled bow / of Vipracitti […]. / As those arrows flew, covering the sun, the powerful / Lord Wind swiftly hurled them down upon the Asuras. / By those arrows of that Daitya, many Dānavas were slain; / and pierced, they wailed on the earth like men dwelling in hell. / Seeing them thus slain, the great Asura Vipracitti / leaped down from his chariot and fought Vāyu in close combat. / As he was engaged in the fight, Vāyu's strength increased, / and the gods thought that Diti's son was subdued. / Then, leaping up swiftly with his mace, the mighty Hiraṇyākṣa / struck Wind firmly upon the region of the cheek.

Then that dānava Virocana, whose chariot had been burned, standing in the sky,
swiftly drew his sword and, full of valor, cut down all the sharp arrows
of Pūṣan as they flew toward him, and his bow as well;
and then he struck him once more on the head with his sword.
Under that severe blow, his head streaming with blood,
[Pūṣan] quickly fell into the chariot-box like a flagstaff after a festival.
Seeing him fallen, that mighty lord of daityas seized him swiftly
and hurled him at the king of the gods, roaring like a raincloud.
And Mitra pierced Bali in the collarbone region with three arrows;
with a single broad-headed shaft, Bali severed his bow.
Then with another he struck him in the heart;
stunned and as if dead, he sank down in the chariot-box.
Vyāsa, fearing death, his charioteer carried him away
as he lay despondent and fallen; then the daityas raised a shout of triumph.

7.9.m: […] / Sanatkumāra said: / Overcome with rage, Maya attacked the god Candramas / with arrows shaped like venomous serpents, roaring like a raincloud. / As he shot his arrows, Candramas, as if smiling, / split each into seven parts and pierced Maya with five. / Then with an arrow he struck him on the forehead, / and the god laughed again, inflicting shame upon him. / As he laughed, [Maya], greatly exerting himself, quickly pierced his forehead / with a heron-feathered shaft, as an obstacle [strikes] one observing a vow. / Then aiming at his banner, the god severed it while making a loud cry, / and with swords he dispatched the wheel-guards to the realm of Yama. / Seeing that dexterity of his, Maya, the foremost of Dānavas, / resorted to divine sorcery and then became Rāhu. / Becoming Rāhu, the lord of Daityas rushed upon the lord of gods, the hare-marked [Moon], / as Rāhu does, with a chariot roaring like a cloud. / Understanding that sorcery, the god born from nectar, / assailed him standing in the sky with three arrows, as if on an unordained conjunction. / But that Daitya, a master of great illusion, warding off those arrows by magic itself, / rushed at the cool-rayed [Moon], a mighty Asura. / Then, seizing by the yoke his divine chariot, radiant and steered by serpents, / the Daitya hurled it and roared aloud.

Sanatkumāra said: / Aryaman with many arrows struck Prahlāda, the bull among Daityas, / [and destroyed] his dread chariot, and felled his banner.
The heroic Prahlāda, abandoning that chariot, / rushed at Aryaman, just as Rāhu [rushes] at the dispenser of darkness in due season.
Aryaman struck with many arrows the enemy charging with speed and without weapons, / just as a cloud [strikes] a mountain with rain.
Paying no heed at all to the arrows, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, / out of wrath, pride, and arrogance, rushed forward with speed.
Seizing the pole of his gold-adorned chariot, / along with the charioteer Citra, he then roared with joy.
Anuhrāda, approaching Dhara, was pierced by him in the chest; / drawing his sword with speed, he approached Dhara's chariot.
Cutting down his banner, horses, charioteer, and bow, / and [striking] Dhara on the shoulder, he returned again to his own chariot.

7.9.m: as snakes [rush upon] Garuḍa, or bees upon a tree, / so all those Dānavas, seizing excellent weapons, // roaring like great rainclouds, charged at the cool-beamed god. / O Vyāsa, as they charged, the enemy of darkness, smiling as it were, // severed with his arrows on every side their uplifted weapons. / Then that god, filled with wrath, once more pierced // all of them in their hearts with sharp arrows and roared aloud. / And with biting cold, the immutable lord of the stars, // his eyes reddened with rage, struck all the asuras. / Pierced by arrows and severely tormented by the cold, // the Daitya lords stood fixed right there, as if painted on canvas. / And the god Candra too, bending his bow into a circle in battle, // pierced all the Daitya lords, roaring like a cloud. / Whichever Dānava or Daitya, O best of sages, // [came forward,] all of them then bore the arrows of the moon. / Whenever a Daitya moved any limb, // right there the god pierced it with sharp arrows and roared. / Wherever in the battle a Daitya warrior spoke, // Candramas struck eight arrows right into his mouth. / Motionless, all those foremost asuras stood like mutes, / all their limbs pierced by arrows, as if painted on canvas. / Just as the divine lord Candramas was the crusher of the Dānavas, / even so the divine lord Fire tormented the Dānavas in battle.
